Hook

How long is the throw from home plate to second base?

A baseball diamond is a square, 90 feet on each side. The catcher throws from home plate to second base, along the diagonal of the square. Nobody measures that line during a game.

How long is that throw? Make an estimate now. By the end of Part 1 you can find it exactly.

The two 90-foot sides meet at first base at a right angle. The throw runs along the dashed line, across from that right angle.

Today's objective

Goals for Part 1

In Part 1 you find missing sides of right triangles.

  • I can point to the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle, in any orientation.
  • I know whether to add or subtract the squares before I start computing.
  • I give an exact radical first, a decimal only when asked.
  • I know the three base triples and their multiples on sight.
The Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse · Unit 1: Triangle Geometry · Section 1.16 / 68
The idea

The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, however the triangle is turned

The two sides that form the right angle are the legs. The side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse, always the longest side.

Label the angles , , , and name the side opposite each angle , , . Put the right angle at , so is the hypotenuse.

The same triangle in two positions. In both, the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle at , even when it lies flat along the bottom.
The Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse · Unit 1: Triangle Geometry · Section 1.17 / 68
The idea

Why the Pythagorean theorem is true: one square frame, two arrangements

Fit four copies of a right triangle, with legs , and hypotenuse , into a square frame with side a+b in two ways.

Left frame: the uncovered area is a tilted square, area . Right frame: two squares, area .

Same frame, same triangles, so the uncovered areas are equal. In every right triangle,

c2=a2+b2
Why the tilted shape on the left is a square: its four sides are each . Each of its corners sits on a side of the frame, between the triangle's two acute angles. Those angles add to , so each corner is 180∘−90∘=90∘..
The Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse · Unit 1: Triangle Geometry · Section 1.18 / 68

Worked example

Find a leg

Worked example: find a leg

When the missing side is a leg, the square of the hypotenuse is the total. Subtract the known leg's square from it.

The ladder is the hypotenuse: length 6, base 2 from the wall, wall height unknown.

The idea

Three base Pythagorean triples to know on sight

A Pythagorean triple is three positive whole numbers , , with .

Multiplying all three numbers by the same whole number scales the triple, and the result is another triple. Each square is multiplied by , so the equation still holds.

Summary

Key ideas

Build the intuition

  • Legs: the two sides that form the right angle.
  • Hypotenuse: the side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side and always the in .
  • Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle, two known sides give the third.
  • Exact answers: give the exact radical first, simplified, and rationalized when a root is in a denominator. Use a decimal only when the problem asks for one.

Build the intuition

Back to the baseball throw: the two 90-foot sides are the legs, so the throw is 902+902​=16200​=902​≈127.279 feet.

Hook

A tape measure can check that a corner is square, with no protractor

A framing crew must make a foundation corner exactly square before the concrete arrives. They mark 3 feet along one edge and 4 feet along the other. Then they measure the diagonal between the two marks.

What diagonal length means the corner is exactly square? Make a prediction. The converse of the Pythagorean theorem, later in Part 2, settles it.

Marks at 3 ft and 4 ft along the two edges, joined by one dashed diagonal.

The Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse · Unit 1: Triangle Geometry · Section 1.140 / 68
The idea

The converse switches the if and the then

The converse of "if P, then Q" is "if Q, then P."

A converse can be false: squares have four sides, but not all four-sided shapes are squares.

The Pythagorean theorem: if angle is right, then .

Its converse is true: if , then angle is right.

A 5-foot diagonal means a square corner: 32+42=52..

The Pythagorean Theorem and Its Converse · Unit 1: Triangle Geometry · Section 1.141 / 68
The idea

Compare the longest side's square with the sum of the other two squares

First check that the lengths form a triangle: the two shorter sides must add to more than the longest. Then let the longest side be , and compare with :

  • equal: the triangle is right
  • less than : the triangle is acute
  • greater than : the triangle is obtuse
Keep sides and and change the angle between them: a wider angle makes longer. That angle is acute when c2<a2+b2,, right when the two are equal, and obtuse when is greater.

The idea

Distance between two points: the Pythagorean theorem in coordinates

The horizontal and vertical distances between two points are the legs of a right triangle. The segment joining the points is the hypotenuse.

The legs are the differences of the x-coordinates and of the y-coordinates, so the distance is

d=(x2​−x1​)2+(y2​−y1​)2​

Squaring removes any minus sign, so the order of the two points does not matter.

The horizontal distance and the vertical distance are the legs; the distance is the hypotenuse.

Summary

Key ideas

The converse: reading angles from sides

  • Converse: start from three side lengths and classify the triangle. First check that the two shorter sides add to more than the longest.
  • Right, acute, or obtuse: with the longest side, compare with . Equal means right, less means acute, and greater means obtuse.

Distance: the theorem in another form

  • Distance formula: the same theorem in coordinates, with the horizontal and vertical distances as the legs.

  • Tell it as a story: the diagonal is a distance no one measures directly, yet every fielder trusts it.
  • Gesture the square: two 90-foot legs meet at a right angle at the base, and the throw is the hypotenuse across.
  • Ask for a gut estimate before any math: more than 90 feet? A lot more? Take three guesses.
  • By the end of Part 1 we can find it exactly: 902​≈127.279 feet, and the summary slide shows it. Exact first, decimal when the field needs it.
  • Right triangles give you a way to find distances a tape measure cannot reach. Surveyors, framers, and coaches all run the same calculation.

The ideaGive it 4 minStart by minute 12Day 1

Say / do

  • This one definition prevents this section's most expensive mistake.
  • Point to the marked right angle, then to the side across from it: that is the hypotenuse, labeled c.
  • Say the naming rule for the whole book. Angles get capital letters A, B, C. The side opposite each gets the matching lowercase a, b, c. Put the right angle at C, so c is the hypotenuse.
  • Physically rotate a paper triangle: opposite the right angle is the definition; slanted is only how it happens to be drawn.
  • Longest side sits opposite the largest angle, and the right angle is the largest in a right triangle, so the hypotenuse is longest.

Watch for

  • Grabbing the slanted-looking side as the hypotenuse in a rotated picture. Cover the tilt and ask only: which side faces the right angle?

Moves

  • Hold up a paper right triangle and rotate it while they track the hypotenuse

Support

Have them mark the right angle and the side across from it before anything else.
The ideaGive it 3 minStart by minute 16Day 1

Say / do

  • You met the theorem in geometry; here is the sixty-second reason it is true, so students see why it holds instead of memorizing it.
  • Left frame: the four triangles sit in the corners and the floor left uncovered is one tilted square with side c, area c squared.
  • Right frame: pair the triangles into two rectangles and the floor left uncovered is two squares, one a by a and one b by b.
  • Same frame, same four triangles, so the uncovered areas must match. That is the whole proof.

Watch for

  • Students taking the tilted shape in the left frame for a square without a reason. Here is why it is one. All four sides are c, and each corner is a straight angle minus the triangle's two acute angles. That leaves a right angle.
  • Reading the frame's side as c. The frame's side is a + b; c is the side of the tilted inner square.

Moves

  • Point and trace: run a finger around the leftover area in each frame
  • Optional hands-on: four paper copies of the triangle from the hypotenuse slide, packed both ways on the desk

Extension

Second proof for a fast finisher: drop the altitude from the right angle to the hypotenuse. Then use the two similar triangles it creates (the book's Dig In box in 1.1).

Support

Count what is covered: four triangles both times. So what is left over has to be the same area both times.

Say / do

  • Let them spot it before you say anything: turn and talk for 60 seconds.
  • The clue is built in: a 13.928 'leg' is longer than the 13 hypotenuse, which no right triangle allows.

Error: the student added, treating the missing leg like a hypotenuse. But 13 is the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle), so its square is the total. Correct: , so . Note 5-12-13 is a base triple, and 12 is shorter than 13, as it must be.

Can skip if short on time

Board practice set; assign the five problems as homework, since the worked examples already model adding and subtracting squares.

Say / do

  • Roll visibly random trios (Grouper or a card draw). One marker per group, rotate the scribe.
  • Release the problems in order: a group starts the next problem only when the one before is done. Here is the one thing that changes. Problems 1 and 2 add for a hypotenuse, and problem 3 switches to subtracting for a leg. Problem 4 adds a radical to simplify, and problem 5 makes them set up two equal legs.
  • Protect struggle: at least 4 minutes on the last two problems before any hint. Answer questions with questions.
  • Point a stuck group toward a group that has finished that problem.
  • Consolidate at the boards for the last two minutes. Walk the class to a board that finished problem 5. Have that group narrate the two equal legs. Land the day's rule: add the squares for a hypotenuse, subtract for a leg, exact radical first.

Watch for

  • On problem 3, adding instead of subtracting. On problem 5, forgetting there are two equal legs, so .

Answers and worked solutions

1. c=32+42​=25​=5 (the 3-4-5 triple).
2. c=52+122​=169​=13 (the 5-12-13 triple).
3. b=252−242​=625−576​=49​=7 (7-24-25 is a triple that is not on the table).
4. b=82−42​=64−16​=48​=43​≈6.928..
5. Two equal legs: , so , , s=50​=52​≈7.071 meters.

Moves

  • Grouper random groups of 3, vertical whiteboards, one marker, rotate scribe
  • Groups work the problems in order
  • Circulate, hints only

Extension

Problem 4 gave a radical that simplifies. Build one that does not: pick a hypotenuse and leg whose difference of squares is prime.

Support

Hint ladder for rung 5: (1) The diagonal cuts the square into two right triangles. (2) Both legs are the same unknown s. (3) So ; solve for s and simplify the radical. If a group writes s2​=10 and reaches s=2​10​,, that is correct but not finished. Have them rationalize by multiplying top and bottom by 2​:: 2102​​=52​.. That is the same answer as the method. Section 2.4 makes rationalizing routine.

HookGive it 3 minStart by minute 2Day 2

Say / do

  • Tell it with stakes: not close, exact, before the truck pours.
  • If the diagonal reads 5 feet, the corner is square. Long means splayed open past a right angle; short means pinched under.
  • Three numbers, one corner, no angle ever measured. That reverse direction has a name: the converse.
  • This is the whole job of the first half of Part 2: read the type of angle from the sides.

Answers and worked solutions

If the diagonal is exactly 5 feet, the corner is right: 32+42=9+16=25=52.. Longer than 5 means obtuse; shorter means acute.

  • Reveal the 3 and 4, ask the class to predict which diagonal makes it square

Say / do

  • First, converse in plain English: exchange the if and the then. So 'If a right angle, then ' becomes 'if , then a right angle'. A statement being true does not make its converse true. Here, though, the converse is true, and it comes with a bonus on the next slide.

The ideaGive it 3 minStart by minute 14Day 2

Say / do

  • Show the included angle: fix the two shorter sides at a corner. Open the corner past a right angle and the far side c stretches; close it and c shrinks. The boundary is exactly .
  • So the direction of the mismatch gives the type: less means the angle is acute, greater means it is obtuse.
  • One check first: the three lengths must form a triangle. The two shorter sides must add to more than the longest, or there is nothing to classify.

Watch for

  • Letting any side play c. c must be the longest, always, or the comparison is meaningless.

Keep the three-line rule visible; it is the whole method.

  • Contrast (b) and (c): same two short sides 4 and 5, but the longest side decides. Side 8 is too long (obtuse), and side 6 is short enough (acute).
  • (d) is the triangle check itself: 2 and 3 cannot reach 9, so there is nothing to classify. The check runs before any squaring.
  • This is the framing crew's test giving all four results, one of them "no triangle at all."

Watch for

  • Comparing the wrong pair; it is always longest-squared versus the sum of the other two squares.
  • Skipping the triangle check. 2, 3, 9 classify nothing because 2+3<9..

Answers and worked solutions

(a) right, since 676=100+576.. (b) obtuse, since . (c) acute, since . (d) no triangle, since 2+3=5<9..

Say / do

  • The converse only speaks about lengths that already close into a triangle. So the first test is not a square at all: do the two shorter sides add to more than the longest?
  • Here 4 + 6 = 10, and 10 is less than 11. The short sides cannot reach each other. No triangle, so nothing to classify.
  • Show the slip: run the converse anyway and 121 against 52 looks like a confident obtuse, a verdict about a triangle nobody can build.

Watch for

  • Squaring first and announcing obtuse. The check runs before the comparison, every time.
  • Adding all three sides, or the two longest. It is the two shorter sides against the longest.

Answers and worked solutions

Triangle check first: the two shorter sides total , and , so the sides cannot close. No triangle at all, and nothing to classify. Running the converse anyway would give against 42+62=16+36=52,, and 121>52 reads as obtuse, a verdict about a triangle that does not exist.
Extension: with 4 and 6 the longest side must be less than , so the largest whole number is 9. Then 92=81 against , and 81>52:: obtuse.

Moves

  • Whole-class thumbs or mini-whiteboards, four possible verdicts
  • If the room says obtuse, reteach the triangle check now: two shorter sides against the longest, before any squaring

Sort the three numbers. Add the two smaller ones. If that total is not greater than the biggest, stop: there is no triangle.

Say / do

  • Build it from what they know: to get from one point to the other, go horizontal then vertical, forming a right triangle.
  • The horizontal distance comes from a difference of x-coordinates; the vertical distance comes from a difference of y-coordinates. Those are the legs.
  • The distance is the hypotenuse, so it is the theorem in coordinates. Squaring erases minus signs, so the order of the points does not matter.
  • Preview the payoff: measured from the origin, points 1 unit out satisfy . That is a circle, and Unit 2 lives on it.

Board task combining distance and the converse; assign it as homework, since nothing later in the lesson uses it.

Say / do

  • Roll fresh random trios, one marker, rotate the scribe.
  • This fuses both of today's skills: distances give the sides, the converse gives the angle. The efficient step is to keep squared lengths and never take a root until the last step, if at all.
  • Protect struggle: let them wrestle with how to combine the two tools before you hint. Hand out the extension only when a group has the main verdict.
  • The satisfying result: the right angle sits at C, invisible until the numbers reveal it.
  • Consolidate at the boards for the last two minutes. Walk the class to a board that kept everything squared. Have that group narrate the verdict. Finish the step: let the largest squared length be c squared, then compare it with the sum of the other two. Never take a square root you do not need.

Watch for

  • Taking square roots too early and drowning in decimals. The converse only needs the squared lengths.
  • Not identifying the longest side as c before comparing; here is largest.

Answers and worked solutions

1. AB=(7−1)2+(3−1)2​=36+4​=40​=210​≈6.325..
2. , BC2=(3−7)2+(5−3)2=16+4=20,, AC2=(3−1)2+(5−1)2=4+16=20..
3. The longest side is AB, so it is c: and . Equal, so right (the right angle is at C).
4. With C(3,6):: AC2=4+25=29,, BC2=16+9=25,, . Now 40<29+25=54,, so acute.

Moves

  • Grouper random groups of 3, vertical whiteboards, one marker, rotate scribe
  • Reveal the extension only after the main verdict
  • Circulate, hints only

Extension

Find coordinates for C that make triangle ABC obtuse. What must be true about then?

Support

Hint ladder: (1) You need the three side lengths; which tool gives a length from two points? (2) Keep them squared, do not take roots. (3) The longest squared length is c-squared; compare it with the sum of the other two.

Classes 2 and 3Two 60-minute classes
Why two classes: Five objectives and three distinct procedures (find a missing side, classify by the converse, find distance in coordinates) cannot each get worked-then-faded practice plus protected struggle time in one 60-minute class. Part 1 runs the theorem forward: right-triangle anatomy, finding a side (add for a hypotenuse, subtract for a leg), and Pythagorean triples. Part 2 runs it backward with the converse (right, acute, obtuse) and into coordinates with the distance formula.

Objective

Use the Pythagorean theorem and its converse to find a missing side, classify a triangle from its three sides, recognize the common triples, and measure the distance between two points.

Big question

How can three side lengths measure a distance you cannot reach and an angle you never touched?

Materials

  • whiteboard markers
  • vertical whiteboards or wall space (Building Thinking Classrooms)
  • handout: practice (take-home, Part 1 and Part 2 sheets)
  • exit ticket slips, Part 1 and Part 2
  • student notebooks
  • a straightedge or ruler
  • graph or grid paper for the distance work (Part 2)
  • calculators, for decimal approximations only
  • a paper right-triangle cutout to rotate (Part 1, naming the sides)

A student found the other leg of a triangle with hypotenuse 10 and leg 8 as . Explain the error. Give the correct answer.

Hook

A drone's position is two numbers

A drone flies a circle of radius 1 kilometer around a tower. At any moment, its position is two numbers: how far east and how far north of the tower. Around the circle, both numbers grow, shrink, and turn negative. When the drone is up and to the left of the tower, is its east number positive or negative?

At any moment, the drone's position is how far east and how far north of the tower it is.

Summary

Key ideas

Build the intuition

  • Unit circle: the circle of radius centered at the origin. It turns sine and cosine from triangle ratios into coordinates.
  • Sine, cosine, and tangent for any angle: the terminal side of crosses the unit circle at . Cosine and come first, and sine and come second.
  • Tangent is the slope of the terminal side: tanθ=cosθsinθ​.. It is undefined where the terminal side stands vertical, where .
Sine, Cosine, and Tangent in Quadrants II, III, and IV · Unit 2: The Unit Circle · Section 2.3Continued on the next slide27 / 75
Summary

Key ideas, continued

Signs by neighborhood

  • Signs of the trig functions by quadrant: cosine copies the sign of , and sine copies the sign of . All three functions are positive in Quadrant I, and each other quadrant has exactly one positive function.
  • All Star Trig Class: counterclockwise from Quadrant I, the positive functions are all three, then sine, then tangent, then cosine.

Summary

Key ideas

The reference angle: one quadrant carries the other three

  • Reference angle: is the acute angle between the terminal side and the horizontal axis. In Quadrants II, III, and IV, it is π−θ,, θ−π,, and 2π−θ..
  • Reference-angle method: the reference angle gives the absolute value; the quadrant gives the sign.
  • Supplement identities: the same mirror symmetry proves and . Section 1.3 borrowed these facts, and Section 2.1 leaned on them.

The ideaGive it 6 minStart by minute 13Day 1

Say / do

  • Define it in one breath: radius 1, centered at the origin. Pythagoras in coordinates says a point at distance 1 satisfies x squared plus y squared equals 1. That is the check you will see in every answer key today. It is also why (5/13, 12/13) with a sign is a valid point and (1/2, 1/2) is not.
  • Start with the acute case on the diagram. Drop a straight line from the point to the x-axis and a right triangle appears, hypotenuse 1 along the radius.
  • Aim SOH-CAH-TOA at it: sine is opposite over hypotenuse, which is y over 1, or y itself. Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, x over 1, or x itself. On the unit circle the dividing does nothing.
  • Here is the big step of the whole section: the definitions now work for every angle. A terminal side pointing into Quadrant II or III has no acute triangle to offer. But it still crosses the circle at a perfectly good point. So we keep the meaning where it works and let the coordinates BE the definition everywhere else.
  • Keep the pairing straight with the alphabet: Cosine and x both come first, Sine and y both come second.

Watch for

  • Students mixing up which coordinate is which; tie it to the alphabet, cos-x first, sin-y second.

Moves

  • choral read: cosine is x, sine is y
  • cold call: on the diagram, point to cosine theta, then to sine theta

Worked exampleGive it 6 minStart by minute 19Day 1

Say / do

  • No memorizing here, ever: sketch the point, read the coordinates. Model that out loud on part (a): a full turn comes back to (1, 0).
  • Part (b) is the one to slow down on. A zero in the numerator (top), as in tan 2 pi, is a fine answer: zero. A zero in the DENOMINATOR (bottom), as in tan of pi halves, is not an answer at all. Division by zero is undefined, and the picture agrees because the terminal side is vertical.
  • Part (c): the two coordinates are the cosine and sine outright. Only the tangent takes a step, and a negative divided by a negative is positive. So the tangent comes out positive, as we will confirm with ASTC later in Part 1.
  • Notice (c) is the warmup triangle with minus signs: same 3, 4, 5 lengths, now in Quadrant III.

Watch for

  • Students calling tan of pi halves zero (reading it like tan 2 pi); the zero is in the DENOMINATOR here, so it is undefined.

(a) cos2π=1, sin2π=0, tan2π=0.. (b) cos2π​=0, sin2π​=1, tan2π​ undefined. (c) cosθ=−54​, sinθ=−53​, tanθ=43​..

The ideaGive it 6 minStart by minute 29Day 1

Say / do

  • Tangent is not a mystery third value; it is the slope of the ray you already drew. Rise over run, y over x, which is sine over cosine.
  • Trace the run and the rise on the diagram with a finger: over by cosine, up by sine. Slope is up over over.
  • Now the undefined case has a picture. When the terminal side stands straight up, there is no run, and x is 0. A vertical line has an undefined slope. That is the geometry of dividing by zero.
  • Flag for later: sine over cosine becomes an official identity in a few sections; today we read it only as the slope.

Watch for

  • Students treating tangent as unrelated to sine and cosine; it is literally their quotient, the slope.

  • choral read: tangent is sine over cosine
  • cold call: where else is tangent undefined besides pi halves? (three pi halves, and any coterminal angle)

Group challengeGive it 11 minStart by minute 38Day 1

Say / do

  • Roll random trios with Grouper, one marker per group, up at the vertical boards. This is a thinking task, not a recall drill: protect at least four minutes of struggle before any hint.
  • Circulate and answer questions with questions: what is the sign of x here? Of y? So what is the sign of their quotient? Do not give away the pattern.
  • Consolidate at the boards: cosine copies the sign of x (negative on the left half). Sine copies the sign of y (negative on the bottom half). Tangent, their quotient, is positive exactly where x and y share a sign.
  • Land the count: All positive in Quadrant I, only Sine in II, only Tangent in III, only Cosine in IV. Tangent is positive in I and III because that is where x and y agree in sign.

Watch for

  • Groups deciding tangent's sign by feel instead of dividing; force them to write y over x with the actual signs.
  • Groups forgetting Quadrant I is all positive because they only look for the single positive one; I is the exception.

Answers and worked solutions

(a) Quadrant I: x>0,y>0,, all three positive. Quadrant II: x<0,y>0,, only sinθ>0 (cosine and tangent negative). Quadrant III: x<0,y<0,, only tanθ>0 (a negative over a negative). Quadrant IV: x>0,y<0,, only cosθ>0..
(b) Tangent is , positive exactly when and share a sign: Quadrants I and III.

The ideaGive it 5 minStart by minute 12Day 2

Say / do

  • Do not memorize the three formulas as separate facts. Each asks one question: how far is the terminal side from the x-axis? In Quadrant II you are short of a half turn; in III you are past it; in IV you are short of a full turn.
  • Say the slip now, before examples: measure to the HORIZONTAL axis, never the vertical. For 120 degrees the angle to the x-axis is 60, and the tempting wrong 30 measured to the y-axis. A sketch settles it.
  • Self-test: a terminal side close to the x-axis, like 175 degrees, must have a tiny reference angle, here 5 degrees. If yours comes out near 90, you measured to the wrong axis.

Watch for

  • The axis slip: measuring theta prime to the nearest axis, including the vertical one, so 120 degrees yields 30 instead of 60. The reference angle is measured to the x-axis, always.

Say / do

  • Here is the key idea of the whole section. The reference angle gives the absolute value; the quadrant gives the sign. Two jobs, kept separate.
  • Insist on the ritual, because it heads off the number one error. Write the sign down FIRST, straight from the quadrant, before a single digit lands on the page. Take cos 120 degrees: it is minus cos 60 degrees. That minus is locked in from Quadrant II before anyone computes 0.5.
  • Why it works: the point at theta is a mirror image of the point at theta prime, and reflections can change signs but never change absolute values. The reference angle carries no sign of its own, ever.
  • So the reference angle only ever supplies digits. It never touches the sign.

Watch for

  • The section's core misconception: using half the method. That means finding theta prime, looking up its positive Quadrant I value, and handing it in sign and all. So cos 120 comes back plus 0.5. The sign comes from the quadrant, not from the reference angle.

Moves

  • choral read: sign from the quadrant, absolute value from the reference angle
  • model the sign-first ritual out loud once

The ideaGive it 3 minStart by minute 37Day 2

Say / do

  • Look back at the examples so far: cos 155 is minus cos 25, cos 120 is minus cos 60. Each pair adds to 180. That is not a coincidence, it is a rule with a name: the supplement identities.
  • Why: the points at theta and 180 minus theta are mirror images across the y-axis. Same y-coordinate, so the sines match. Opposite side, so the cosines have opposite signs.
  • This pays two debts. Lesson 3 borrowed 'an obtuse angle has a negative cosine' for the Law of Cosines. Here is why it holds: an obtuse angle lands in Quadrant II, where x is negative. Lesson 4's ambiguous case kept finding a second triangle at 180 minus B. The supplement has the same sine, so the calculator could not tell the two apart.
  • Cold call, no calculator: write sin 150 and cos 150 in terms of 30 degrees, signs included.

Watch for

  • Students reading the rule as 'the supplement changes every sign': only cosine changes sign. Send them to the reflection: the y-coordinate stays, the x-coordinate changes sign.
  • Students applying 180 minus theta to a Quadrant III or IV angle. The supplement rule is the Quadrant II row of the reference-angle table, nothing more.

Answers and worked solutions

150∘=180∘−30∘,, so sin150∘=sin30∘=0.5 and cos150∘=−cos30∘≈−0.866.. Check with the reference-angle method: Quadrant II, , sine positive, cosine negative; same two answers.

Moves

  • choral read: same sine, opposite cosine
  • cold call two students for the 150 degree check

Extension

Use the mirror across the x-axis instead and predict , ; check with θ=40∘ on a calculator (sin(−40∘)≈−0.643,, cos(−40∘)≈0.766).

Support

Draw the points for 30 degrees and 150 degrees on one unit circle and mark the y-coordinate of each: the same segment, mirrored.
The ideaGive it 4 minStart by minute 40Day 2

Say / do

  • Two loose ends. First, real wheels are not radius 1. A circle of radius r is the unit circle scaled up, so every coordinate multiplies by r. The point is r cosine theta, r sine theta.
  • The height pattern is worth keeping: fixed hub height k plus r sine theta. That exact shape returns as the star of Unit 3's wave models.
  • Second, stray angles. A negative angle or one past a full turn still has a terminal side. So replace it with its coterminal angle in first, then proceed. Coterminal angle first, reference-angle method second.

Watch for

  • Students using the method on a raw angle like 595 degrees; subtract the full turn first, then evaluate the leftover.
  • Students writing for a point off the unit circle; is a length coordinate, and only when is it the sine. Otherwise divide by .

Moves

  • choral read: point is r cosine theta, r sine theta
  • cold call: find the angle in [0, 360) degrees coterminal with 595 degrees (595 minus 360 is 235)

Watch for

Classes 13 and 14Two 60-minute classes
Why two classes: Part 1 builds the coordinate definition (sine, cosine, and tangent as the y, x, and slope of the point on the unit circle), the quadrantal values, and the ASTC sign rule discovered from the signs of x and y. Part 2 handles absolute values: the reference angle, the reference-angle method (the reference angle gives the absolute value, the quadrant gives the sign), coterminal reduction, and points on a wheel of radius r. Five objectives, the coordinate redefinition, the sign rule, reference angles, and the section's sign misconception are far too much to teach with real struggle time and consolidation in one 60-minute class.

Objective

Read sine and cosine as coordinates on the unit circle, name the sign of any angle from its quadrant (mnemonic: ASTC, All Star Trig Class), and evaluate anywhere with the reference angle for the absolute value and the quadrant for the sign.

Big question

Once an angle is too big for a triangle, how does one circle give it a sine, a cosine, and a tangent, with the right sign?

Materials

  • whiteboard markers and vertical whiteboards
  • handout (Sine, Cosine, and Tangent in Quadrants II, III, and IV, practice), take-home: the Part 1 sheet after Part 1, the Part 2 sheet after Part 2
  • exit ticket slips for Part 1 and Part 2
  • Grouper (or the offline roller) for random trios
  • calculators (degree and radian mode)
  • blank four-quadrant and unit-circle sketch templates
  • protractors (optional, for sketching angles and reference angles)

Unit 3: Periodic Functions · Section 3.1

Graphing Sine and Cosine, Part 1

A point travels around the unit circle. If you graph its y-coordinate against the angle it has turned, what shape do you get?

It's oscillations of constant height.The Other Zoey (2023)
Unit 3: Periodic Functions · Section 3.11 / 72
Hook

The height of one blade tip, graphed over time, is a wave

Watch one wind turbine across a field. Track a single blade tip: it climbs, eases over the top, sweeps down, skims the bottom, and climbs again. The same rise and fall repeats over and over.

There is no triangle here, but that repeating height still comes from trigonometry. Today you'll build that wave from the unit circle.

Today's objective

Read the sine and cosine graphs off the unit circle

Goal: read the sine and cosine graphs off the unit circle

By the end of Part 1 you can:

  • explain how the y-coordinate of a point on the unit circle becomes the sine curve, and its x-coordinate becomes the cosine curve;
  • state the period, range, and amplitude of both curves;
  • evaluate sine and cosine at far-away and negative angles using periodicity and the even and odd identities.
Graphing Sine and Cosine · Unit 3: Periodic Functions · Section 3.17 / 72
The idea

Sine is the y-coordinate of point P, graphed against the angle

Point is where the terminal side of meets the unit circle. As grows, graph the y-coordinate of against . That graph is the sine curve. The x-coordinate, graphed the same way, is the cosine curve.

The graph's horizontal axis is not the circle's x-axis. It measures , the distance has traveled, in radians.

The y-coordinate of point P (left), its height above the horizontal axis, becomes the y-value of the graph (right). On the unit circle the arc length is s=rθ=θ,, since . So the horizontal axis measures the arc length P has traveled.

The idea

Period, range, and symmetry of the sine and cosine graphs

  • Period : both graphs repeat every , since one full turn returns to the same point: , .
  • Range : stays on the unit circle. Amplitude : half the distance from maximum to minimum.
  • , so cosine is even; , so sine is odd.
  • Domain: all real numbers.
The angles and −θ (a negative angle turns clockwise) give points that are mirror images across the horizontal axis. They have the same x-coordinate, so cosine is even. Their y-coordinates have opposite signs, so sine is odd. The double arrow shows the range: y stays in .

The idea

Five key points: split one period into four equal quarters

Split one period, , into four quarter periods of . The quarter-period points are .

At each one, is on an axis, so the curve is at a maximum, a minimum, or on the midline . Those five points on the curve are the five key points. Plot and join them with one smooth curve.

One period of with its five key points at , equally spaced along the horizontal axis. Their y-values, , come from the unit circle. The midline, , is the horizontal line halfway between the maximum and the minimum.

The cosine curve is the sine curve shifted left by

cosθ=sin(θ+2π​)

Shift the sine curve left by , a quarter period, and it matches the cosine curve exactly. Check at : cos0=1 and .

Why: a point a quarter turn ahead of is at angle . Its y-coordinate always equals the x-coordinate of .

Proof (cofunction identity, then even identity): sin(θ+2π​)=sin(2π​−(−θ))=cos(−θ)=cosθ..

The graph of is the graph of shifted left by : its maximum comes a quarter period sooner. The bracket marks the shift of .

Summary

Key ideas

Sketching one period: the five key points

  • Five key points: one every quarter period, each at a maximum point, a minimum point, or a midline crossing. For sine they are , (2π​,1),, (π,0),, (23π​,−1),, and .
  • Sine versus cosine: sine starts on its midline and increases, and cosine starts at a maximum.

Cosine is sine, shifted left

  • Cosine is a shifted sine: . The cosine graph is the sine graph shifted left a quarter period.
Graphing Sine and Cosine · Unit 3: Periodic Functions · Section 3.1Continued on the next slide63 / 72
Summary

Key ideas, continued

Reading the graph backward

  • Reading a graph backward: each point on the wave gives the position of on the circle. The first coordinate is how far traveled. The second is its -coordinate on the sine graph, or its -coordinate on the cosine graph.

The ideaGive it 5 minStart by minute 10Day 1

Say / do

  • Do the unrolling demo with your hands. Trace the circle with one finger while the other hand drags that y-coordinate straight out to the right along the tape-measure axis.
  • Say it and have them say it back: the number under the wave answers how far the point has traveled around the circle, never where the point is.
  • The horizontal axis is time, or arc length traveled, in radians. It is not the circle's x-axis. This is the single idea the whole section rests on.
  • On the unit circle arc length equals angle, s=rθ with . That is why the axis under the wave speaks radians and nothing else. So a bare number under a wave is radians: means the sine of radians. That is about 0.909,, nowhere near sin2∘≈0.035..

Watch for

  • The headline misconception: reading the wave's horizontal axis as the circle's own x-axis. That leads to sketching sine as a chain of half-circle arcs, and to filing sine and cosine as two unrelated shapes.
  • Fix in the moment: run one full turn of the demo. Point out that the y-coordinate on the circle becomes the y-value on the graph, unchanged.
  • Anyone who plots with a calculator in degree mode gets a nearly horizontal, wrong graph. Radian mode first, and run Unit 1's mode check the other way: must return exactly 0.5..

Moves

  • turn and talk: what does the number under the wave measure?

Extension

Ask a fast thinker to predict the cosine curve's value at (1, from the far-right point) before Part 2 gets there.

Support

Give a stuck student the printed unit circle and have them physically slide a ruler from point P out to the graph.

The ideaGive it 5 minStart by minute 24Day 1

Say / do

  • Name it before we use it. A function is a periodic function if some positive number has for every . That is, the outputs repeat, in full, every units of input. The period is the smallest such positive number. For sine and cosine one full turn works, p=2π.. The extension on this slide proves nothing smaller does.
  • Each fact falls out of the circle in a sentence. Period: theta and theta plus 2 pi are one full turn apart, so they land on the same point with the same coordinates.
  • Range: every point sits on a circle of radius one, so neither coordinate can have absolute value greater than one. Amplitude is half the distance from maximum to minimum, which is one.
  • Even and odd: theta and negative theta are mirror images across the horizontal axis, same x, opposite y. That is exactly the odd and even behavior from the warmup: cosine acts like x squared, sine acts like x cubed.
  • Domain comes first in the book's table. You can walk any angle, forward or backward, so every real number is allowed. The range is where geometry bites.

Watch for

  • The even-odd sign slip: dropping the minus sign inside sine. Sine is odd, so and the sign comes out front. Cosine is even, so .
  • If a hand vote says sin(-theta) equals sin(theta), that is the even/odd confusion; counter with the mirror picture in 30 seconds.

Moves

  • turn and talk: which one keeps the minus and which one drops it?

Extension

Prove nothing smaller than 2 pi can be a period for sine (hint: sine reaches 1 only once per full turn).

Support

Draw the horizontal-axis mirror for one angle and read the two coordinates aloud.

Say / do

  • The worked example found the maximum points and zeros on one full turn. Periodicity says the same points come back every full turn, so the list never ends. The +2πn tail is how you write a list that never ends: stands for any integer, one full turn per step, negative turns too.
  • Maximum points of sine: . It is the coterminal angles from 2.2 written as one formula.
  • Zeros of sine come every half turn, at and , so their formula steps by , not : . Cosine's zeros are the same pattern a quarter turn over: .
  • Hold on to this. Section 3.6 is built on it: find every angle that solves this equation.

Watch for

  • Writing θ=2π​+2π and stopping. That is one extra full turn, not all of them; the is the whole point, and it runs through the negative integers too.
  • Giving the zeros of sine as . That skips , , and every odd multiple of a half turn; the zeros step by .

Answers and worked solutions

Maximum points of : , any integer. Check: give , , , each coterminal with , the top of the circle, where the y-coordinate is .
Zeros of : , any integer. Check: 0,π,2π,−π all end on the horizontal axis, where the y-coordinate is .
Cold call, cosine's zeros: ; n=0,1 give and , the top and bottom of the circle.

Moves

  • mini whiteboards: everyone holds up an answer on my count
  • cold call: what does n=−1 give for the maximum points, and where on the circle is it?
  • cold call: the formula for cosine's zeros

Extension

Write every minimum point and every maximum point of cosine as formulas: minimum points , maximum points , any integer.

Support

Start with the list: , then 2π​+2π,, then 2π​+2⋅2π.. What changes from one to the next? Replace the number of full turns with .

Say / do

  • Marker Mode. Roll visibly random groups of three with Grouper, one marker per group, silent rotating scribe, stand at the boards.

Answers and worked solutions

We need . In one full turn the y-coordinate is twice: Quadrant I at and Quadrant II at (same y-coordinate, mirrored across the vertical axis). Periodicity adds one full turn for : and . Four angles: 6π​, 65π​, 613π​, 617π​.. On the graph, the line cuts each hump once going up and once coming down, twice per period.

  • Students who want to plot twenty points. The whole point is that five is enough.

  • read the success criteria aloud
The ideaGive it 5 minStart by minute 11Day 2

Say / do

  • A quarter period is the period over four. For a period of 2 pi that is pi over 2. So the quarter-period points are 0, pi over 2, pi, 3 pi over 2, and 2 pi.
  • The y-values are not guessed, they are read off the circle: 0, 1, 0, negative 1, 0 for sine.
  • Between the marks the shape is a smooth swell, steepest at the midline crossings and flattest at the maximum and minimum points.

Watch for

  • The headline slip in a second form: spacing the five points evenly up the vertical axis instead of along the horizontal axis. Or drawing half-circle arcs between them.
  • Reinforce the check: at the true curve is already at one half, not up near a half-circle arc's 0.75.

Moves

  • turn and talk: what is a quarter period for a period of 2 pi?

Extension

What are the five key points if the period were pi instead of 2 pi? (Quarter-period points 0, , , 3pi/4, pi.)

Support

Give graph paper with the five vertical lines already drawn; students only need to place the five y-values.
Worked exampleGive it 5 minStart by minute 16Day 2

Say / do

  • Pose each part, then show the steps on the Check your work slide. The key contrast with sine: at , cosine is at its maximum, and sine is on the midline, increasing.
  • Part (b) is the payoff of periodicity: you never plot the second period, you copy the first and shift it right by 2 pi.
  • Draw the curve slowly and out loud, steep through the zeros, nearly horizontal at the maximum and minimum.

Watch for

  • Drawing cosine as if its value at were zero, like sine. Cosine's value there is 1, from the far-right point of the circle.

Answers and worked solutions

Five key points of y=cosθ:: (0,1), (2π​,0), (π,−1), (23π​,0), (2π,1).. Extension on [2π,4π]:: (2π,1), (25π​,0), (3π,−1), (27π​,0), (4π,1)..

Moves

  • pose each part, then show its answer on the Check your work slide
  • signal the first point in a second color

Extension

Sketch a third period on [4pi, 6pi] the same way (slide right by 2 pi again).

Support

Give the five vertical grid lines and have them place 1, 0, −1, 0, 1 as y-values.

Answers and worked solutions

Quarter-period points . Sine is the y-value: (2π,0), (25π​,1), (3π,0), (27π​,−1), (4π,0).. Begin on the midline, increasing, and reach the maximum at . Come back to the midline at , reach the minimum at , and reach the midline again at . Shape check: .

Check your workGive it 0 minStart by minute 26Day 2
Check your workGive it 0 minStart by minute 26Day 2
CheckGive it 3 minStart by minute 26Day 2

Say / do

  • This is the section's headline mistake. Thumbs up if you can spot it, then we reveal.
  • The fix is the check at pi over 6. At pi over 6, only a third of the way to the maximum, the real curve is already at one half.
  • A half-circle arc leaves the axis straight up and stays nearly level near its maximum. So it rides too high at pi over 6. The fix runs the other way: ease the crossings to a finite slope and turn over more sharply at the maximum.

Watch for

  • Students who think the half-circle arc is fine because it hits the same five points. It passes through them but bulges wrong in between.

Answers and worked solutions

The true value is , not . A half-circle arc leaves the axis with a vertical tangent and stays nearly level near its maximum. So a third of the way to the maximum it has already increased to about of the maximum value. Meanwhile the real curve is at exactly . The fix runs the other way from the sketch: ease the crossings to a finite slope and turn over more sharply at the maximum. That pulls the shoulder at down to .

Moves

  • whole-class thumbs check
  • find-the-error reveal

Extension

What does the half-circle arc read at , and what should it be? (The true value is /2, about 0.87.)

Support

Have them plot only the single point (, ) and see it sits below their half-circle arc.

The ideaGive it 4 minStart by minute 29Day 2

Say / do

  • Start a second point a quarter turn ahead of point P. From then on, its y-coordinate matches the x-coordinate of P. That is why cosine is sine shifted left by pi over 2.
  • The second point is the picture. The proof is three steps with two identities you already know. Rewrite the argument as a complement, θ+2π​=2π​−(−θ).. Apply the cofunction identity from 2.4, sin(2π​−(−θ))=cos(−θ).. Then let the even rule absorb the minus, . So sin(θ+2π​)=cosθ at every angle, not only the ones we check.
  • Reading backward is equally useful. Pick any point on the wave: its y-value is one coordinate of point P at that instant.
  • This shift idea pays off again in 3.2 when phase shift arrives.

Watch for

  • Shifting the wrong way. Adding pi over 2 inside the function slides the graph left, not right. Check it at one point if unsure.

Moves

  • turn and talk: which direction does adding inside shift the graph?

Extension

Prove the other direction, cos(θ−2π​)=sinθ,, with the same two identities: θ−2π​=−(2π​−θ),, evenness drops the sign, and the cofunction identity finishes, cos(2π​−θ)=sinθ.. Check at θ=32π​:: both sides are .

Support

Test the identity at theta equals 0: cos 0 is 1, and sin() is 1, so they match.

  • Say the big idea: a graph and the circle are two views of the same walk.

Watch for

  • Thinking the reading-backward answer is a single number; it is a coordinate pair, point P.

Answers and worked solutions

(a) and , equal, so the shift checks out. (b) Point P was : the graph's y-value is the -coordinate, and x=cos3π​=21​..

Say / do

  • Marker Mode again. Visibly random groups of three from Grouper, one marker, silent rotating scribe, at the boards.
  • Protect the struggle time. Circulate and answer questions with questions; point a stuck group toward a group that has a crossing.
  • This ties the whole lesson together: both graphs, exact values, and the circle picture in one task.
  • The pre-marked axes are the time saver: the quarter-period points are already on the strip. So sketching is placing the ten key points and joining them, about two minutes. If a group is still building axes at minute three, hand them a fresh strip.

Watch for

  • Finding only the Quadrant I crossing at and missing the Quadrant III one at 5pi/4.
  • Reading crossings off a sloppy sketch. Push them to the circle: sin equals cos where the point sits on the line y equals x.

Answers and worked solutions

(a) They cross where : and . (b) Shared values: , and . (c) The curves cross where the y-coordinate of point P equals its x-coordinate. That is where on the unit circle: once in Quadrant I at , once in Quadrant III at .

Rung 1: crossing means the two values are equal; write that as an equation. Rung 2: on the circle, when does the y-coordinate equal the x-coordinate? Rung 3: that is the line y = x; where does it hit the unit circle?

Classes 22 and 23Two 60-minute classes
Why two classes: The split falls between reading and evaluating the waves (Part 1) and sketching them by hand (Part 2). Part 1 unrolls the circle into the two curves and uses periodicity and the even-odd identities to evaluate far-away and negative angles. Part 2 uses the five key points to sketch a full period, connects cosine to sine as a quarter-period shift, and reads a graph backward. Each Part is a full 60 minutes with its own warmup, Dig Deeper, and exit ticket.

Objective

Unroll the spinning unit circle into the graphs of sine and cosine, then evaluate them with identities and sketch them by hand from five key points.

Big question

A point travels around the unit circle. If you graph its y-coordinate against the angle it has turned, what shape do you get?

Materials

  • vertical whiteboards
  • one marker per group
  • printed unit circle
  • graph paper
  • handout: Graphing Sine and Cosine, practice
  • exit ticket slips
  • pre-marked axis strips for the Part 2 group task (quarter-period points at pi/2, pi, 3pi/2, 2pi; one per board)

Movie moment

The Other Zoey ↗ (2023), used as hook
"It's oscillations of constant height."
The Other Zoey (2023); via Oliver Knill's Math in Movies clip (Harvard), educational classroom use. In charades, an arm sweeping up and down means sine wave. Quote from the Whisper transcript of the clip.
